title: Suspected bacterial meningitis at 44 with type 2 diabetes, on vancomycin and ceftriaxone without ampicillin

provenance.author: Claude Code (draft for owner review), Listeria risk-factor rule (owner decision 2026-11-12)

story: A 44-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin, not otherwise immunocompromised, presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and new confusion. Lumbar puncture shows a neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose and high protein. Empiric vancomycin, ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 hours and dexamethasone are started; CSF and blood cultures are pending. Ampicillin is not ordered.

expected_findings.summary: Empiric therapy for suspected bacterial meningitis in a patient with diabetes lacks ampicillin: cephalosporins and vancomycin do not cover Listeria monocytogenes.

reference_answer: Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours (12 g a day; a full first dose, then longer intervals in renal impairment) to vancomycin, ceftriaxone and dexamethasone until cultures exclude Listeria; with a serious penicillin allergy, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the usual alternative. Narrow therapy when cultures return.
rationale: ESCMID 2016 names diabetes mellitus among the Listeria risk factors for which amoxicillin or ampicillin is added at any adult age; WHO 2025 lists it too. Diabetes alone discriminates Listeria from pneumococcal meningitis poorly, so this is a guideline-based finding with a modest effect; it tests that the rule reads a risk factor other than immunosuppression.

citations.supports: Empiric amoxicillin or ampicillin for Listeria, added to cefotaxime or ceftriaxone, in adults over 50 and in adults 18 to 50 with Listeria risk factors (Table 4.1 footnote: diabetes mellitus, immunosuppressive drugs, cancer, other immunocompromising conditions).
Add ampicillin or amoxicillin to the initial empiric regimen with any Listeria risk factor, including diabetes mellitus; checked against the WHO document, 2026-11-12.
